Surviving the Performance Review — and t: 职场工作
一次绩效评估、一轮传闻中的裁员,与一次出乎意料的内部转岗:职场沉浮中的三条生存法则。
B2

The email arrived on a Tuesday, sunny and sinister in the way only corporate calendars can be: "Your annual performance review — 45 minutes, Thursday 14:00." I had survived two of these before, but this year felt different. The business had lost its biggest client in the spring, and the corridor conversations had acquired a new grammar — lowered voices, doors closing, the phrase "restructuring" used with the casualness of weather talk. My probation period was long behind me, my projects had shipped on time, and still I spent Wednesday night composing lists of my own achievements like a lawyer preparing for a trial where I was both defendant and counsel.

The review itself was almost disarmingly normal. My line manager — calm, fair, allergic to drama — walked through the standard form: objectives met, feedback gathered, development goals for the year ahead. Then she asked a question no form contains: "If the worst happened here, what would you want to do next?" It was not cruelty; it was a kindness disguised as a hypothetical. The rumours, she could not confirm, concerned a round of redundancies across two departments, mine included. What she could do was make sure that when decisions were made, my file contained evidence, not vibes.

Evidence, it turns out, is a discipline best started years before you need it. That evening I began what I still call the "smug file": every compliment from a client, every chart showing a metric that improved, every time I had covered a sick colleague's shift without being asked. The exercise felt ridiculous until I watched a colleague — talented, modest, and entirely undocumented — struggle to fill in the application for an internal role. He had rebuilt the company's invoicing system almost single-handed, yet sat before a blank form genuinely unable to name a single result, because in his mind the work had simply been "the job". We spent two evenings excavating his memory together, translating projects into outcomes and outcomes into numbers, and he has kept his own file ever since. Talent that cannot describe itself is invisible to decision-makers in a hurry, and restructuring months are nothing if not months of hurry.

The announcement, when it came the following month, was handled better than the rumours had feared. Yes, there would be a layoff programme: eleven roles, voluntary terms first, and a promise — later kept — of no compulsory departures before Christmas. The company offered retraining budgets and, crucially, internal mobility before external hiring. I applied for a transfer to the data team, the smug file now a genuine portfolio, and spent the strangest fortnight of my career being interviewed by people who had spent two years nodding at me in the lift. The offer arrived on a Friday; I accepted before my tea went cold, then walked back past my old desk and felt, for the first time in six weeks, the specific lightness of a decision that had already been made well.

The experience taught me three things worth more than the salary rise that came with the new role. First, performance reviews are not verdicts but evidence hearings, and the evidence is your job all year round. Second, when a workplace trembles, the people who thrive are rarely the loudest; they are the ones whose value can be read from a page. Third — and this surprised me most — loyalty in a company is not repaid with guarantees. It is repaid with information, if you have a manager brave enough to share it. My manager's illegal-to-confirm hint gave me a three-week head start, and three weeks of quiet preparation beat three months of panic.

I still keep the smug file. It takes four minutes on a Friday afternoon, and it has outlasted two restructurings, one merger and a change of desk four buildings wide. Colleagues tease me about it, usually in a whisper, usually the week before their own review. I have stopped counting how many of them now keep one too. Careers, I have decided, are long games played in short rounds, and the rounds you win are the ones you prepared for while everyone else was still listening to rumours instead of writing anything down.
